blogPosts.author: GHL Prime Team
blogPosts.excerpt: GoHighLevel vs HighLevel confuses almost everyone. Here is the plain-English explainer of why one platform has three names, and where LeadConnector shows up.
blogPosts.content:
If you have spent any time around this platform, you have probably been confused at least once. You signed up for ‘GoHighLevel’, but the company calls itself ‘HighLevel’, your text messages show up as ‘LeadConnector’, and you cannot find your account anywhere in Zapier under the name you expected. So what is going on, and which one is the real one?

The short answer: GoHighLevel, HighLevel, and LeadConnector are all the same platform. They are three names for one product, used in different places for deliberate reasons. Once you understand the logic behind the naming, every confusing label suddenly makes sense. Let’s clear it up properly.

GoHighLevel vs HighLevel: which name is correct?

Both are correct — they just come from different places.

  • HighLevel is the official company and product name. The business operates at highlevel.com, and that is the brand you will see on invoices, in legal terms, and in official announcements.
  • GoHighLevel (or GHL) is the original domain name and the name the entire community uses. The platform first launched on gohighlevel.com, and that name stuck. Today almost everyone — agencies, consultants, YouTubers, Facebook groups — says ‘GoHighLevel’ or just ‘GHL’.

So when you ask ‘is GoHighLevel the same as HighLevel?’, the answer is yes, completely. There is no difference in features, pricing, or accounts. It is the same login, the same dashboard, the same tool. HighLevel is simply the tidier official brand; GoHighLevel is the name that history and habit gave it. You can use either and nobody will misunderstand you.

So why is GoHighLevel called LeadConnector?

This is where most people get tripped up, and it is the most interesting part of the story. LeadConnector is a third name, but it is not a different company or a different product. It is HighLevel’s neutral, white-label brand — the identity the platform wears when it needs to stay invisible.

Here is the reason it exists. HighLevel was built as a white-label-first platform. Its core customers are agencies who resell the software to their own clients under their own brand. An agency might sell ‘Acme Marketing CRM’ to a local dentist, and that dentist should never see the words ‘HighLevel’ or ‘GoHighLevel’ anywhere. If they did, the agency’s branding would fall apart and the client could simply go buy the platform directly.

To make that possible, HighLevel uses the neutral name LeadConnector for all the public-facing infrastructure that an agency cannot fully customise. It is a deliberately generic name that gives nothing away.

Where you actually encounter LeadConnector

LeadConnector is not something you choose or sign up for separately. It appears automatically in specific places. Here is where you will run into it.

  • The mobile app. The default app in the App Store and Google Play is called ‘LeadConnector’. It is the same app as the HighLevel mobile app, just neutrally branded so agency clients can download it without seeing the parent name. (Agencies can pay extra for a fully custom-branded app under their own name.)
  • Email and SMS sending. The built-in communication services are branded ‘LC Email’ and ‘LC Phone’ — LC standing for LeadConnector. These are HighLevel’s own sending infrastructure, replacing third-party tools like Mailgun and Twilio.
  • Caller ID and texting. When a message or call goes out and the number has not been verified to a custom name, recipients may see ‘LeadConnector’ on caller ID or in message records. That is simply the platform’s neutral identity showing through.
  • Integration listings. In Zapier, Make, and similar tools, the app is listed as ‘LeadConnector’ — not ‘GoHighLevel’. This is the single most common reason people think their integration is missing.

Common confusions, answered plainly

Why does my texting show LeadConnector?

Because LC Phone is the sending service powering your texts, and ‘LeadConnector’ is its neutral brand. It is not a different company intercepting your messages — it is HighLevel’s own infrastructure. With proper number registration and branded sender setup, you can reduce or remove that label so your business name shows instead.

Why can’t I find GoHighLevel in Zapier?

Because it is not listed under that name. Search Zapier for ‘LeadConnector’ instead, and you will find it immediately. Same platform, neutral listing name. This trips up almost everyone the first time they try to connect an automation.

Is LeadConnector a scam or is it legit?

It is completely legit. LeadConnector is HighLevel — the same company, the same platform, just wearing its white-label name. If you see charges, apps, or messages branded ‘LeadConnector’ and you use GoHighLevel, that is expected and normal, not a sign of fraud.

A quick FAQ

Is GoHighLevel the same as HighLevel?

Yes. Identical platform. HighLevel is the official name; GoHighLevel is the original domain and community name.

Do I need to choose between HighLevel, GoHighLevel, and LeadConnector?

No. You sign up for one platform and get all three identities depending on context. There is nothing to pick.

Will my clients see ‘HighLevel’ anywhere?

If you set up white-label branding correctly, no. That is the entire point of the LeadConnector layer — it keeps the parent name hidden so your brand stays front and centre.

The takeaway

One platform, three names: HighLevel (official), GoHighLevel / GHL (community and original domain), and LeadConnector (the neutral white-label brand for apps, sending, and integrations). The naming feels messy until you see the logic — it is built so agencies can resell the software invisibly. Once you know that, every confusing label becomes a feature, not a bug.

Getting these pieces configured correctly — LC Phone and Email set up, sender branding clean, and white-label branding airtight so your clients never see the wrong name — is exactly where a proper build pays off. If you’re weighing up GoHighLevel, the first question is always the same: how much does it actually cost? The headline plans are simple enough — three tiers — but the subscription is only part of the picture. There are usage charges, add-ons, and an AI layer that can quietly add up. This guide gives you the honest version of GoHighLevel pricing in 2026 so you can pick the right plan the first time.

Quick caveat before we start: prices move. The numbers below are accurate at the time of writing, but always confirm the current figures on the official GoHighLevel site before you commit.

The three main GoHighLevel plans

GoHighLevel sells one platform at three price points. The features overlap heavily — what changes between tiers is how many sub-accounts you get and whether you can run it as your own software business.

Starter — around $97/mo

The entry plan gives you the full GoHighLevel toolkit: CRM, funnels and websites, email and SMS marketing, calendars, pipelines, automation, and reputation management. The catch is scale — Starter caps you at up to three sub-accounts and does not include white-label branding or rebilling.

  • Best for: a solo operator or small business running their own marketing, or an agency with one or two clients testing the waters.
  • The ceiling: you hit the sub-account limit fast once you start onboarding clients.

Unlimited — around $297/mo

This is the workhorse agency plan. The defining feature is in the name: unlimited sub-accounts. You can add as many client accounts as you like without your platform cost going up. You also unlock white-label branding and rebilling at cost — you can pass usage charges (SMS, email, AI) through to clients without applying a markup.

  • Best for: agencies actively managing multiple clients who need room to grow.
  • The upgrade trigger: the moment you outgrow three sub-accounts, $297 almost always beats stacking Starter limits.

Agency Pro / SaaS Pro — around $497/mo

This is where GoHighLevel becomes a business model, not just a tool. SaaS Pro unlocks SaaS Mode: you package GoHighLevel under your own brand, set your own subscription tiers, and resell it as software. It also adds the features that make that viable — rebilling with markup (so usage becomes a profit margin, not just a pass-through), advanced API access, and the white-label desktop and mobile apps.

  • Best for: agencies and founders who want recurring SaaS revenue under their own name.
  • The upgrade trigger: you want SaaS Mode, automated client sign-up and billing, or the ability to mark up usage costs.

The real costs beyond the subscription

This is the part most pricing pages gloss over. Your monthly plan covers the platform — it does not cover usage. Several services are billed separately from a prepaid wallet, and they apply on every plan.

  • SMS and phone: texts, calls, and phone numbers are pay-as-you-go on top of your subscription.
  • Email: sends are metered, so high-volume email campaigns carry a usage cost.
  • AI usage: Conversation AI, Voice AI, and content tools draw from your AI wallet per use.
  • Rebilling math: on Unlimited you can rebill these at cost; on SaaS Pro you can add a markup and keep the difference.

Add-ons and the AI Employee

GoHighLevel also sells the AI Employee — a bundle of Voice AI, Conversation AI, Reviews AI, and content tools. It’s an add-on, not part of the base plan, and it’s priced per sub-account: roughly $50/mo for the Growth tier or about $97/mo for Unlimited usage on each enabled location. That last detail matters — if you turn it on for ten clients, you’re paying for ten, not one. Budget for it deliberately rather than switching it on everywhere by default.

Trial and annual discounts

There’s a 14-day free trial with full access, so you can build and test before paying. There is no permanently free plan — only the trial. If you already know you’re committing, paying annually typically saves you roughly 17% versus monthly billing across all three tiers. Again, confirm the exact discount on the official site, as promotions change.

Which GoHighLevel plan should you choose?

Skip the feature-by-feature paralysis. In practice, the decision comes down to who you are.

  • Solo or small business: Starter at ~$97 is plenty. You get the full platform and you don’t need sub-accounts you’ll never use.
  • Growing agency: Unlimited at ~$297 is the obvious home. Unlimited sub-accounts and white-label branding pay for themselves once you have a handful of clients.
  • Reseller / SaaS founder: SaaS Pro at ~$497 is the only tier that makes sense. SaaS Mode, rebilling with markup, and advanced API turn the platform into a revenue engine.

A simple rule: pick the cheapest plan that doesn’t block your business model. Don’t pay for SaaS Mode you won’t use — but don’t cripple your agency on Starter to save $200 either.

Frequently asked questions

Is there a free GoHighLevel plan?

No. There’s a 14-day free trial with full access, but no permanently free tier. After the trial you move onto one of the paid plans.

What is SaaS Pro?

SaaS Pro (the Agency Pro plan at ~$497/mo) unlocks SaaS Mode, letting you rebrand and resell GoHighLevel as your own software with your own pricing, automated sign-up and billing, rebilling with markup, and advanced API access.

Can I upgrade later?

Yes. You can start on Starter or Unlimited and move up when you hit a real ceiling — outgrowing sub-accounts, or wanting SaaS Mode and markup rebilling. There’s no need to overbuy on day one.

If you are searching for what it costs to hire a GoHighLevel expert, you have probably already discovered that quotes are all over the map. One person says ‘$15 an hour’ and another quotes a five-figure project for what sounds like the same thing. The truth is that GoHighLevel work spans everything from a quick snapshot install to a full SaaS Mode launch with custom development — and the price reflects that range.

This guide breaks down the three realistic ways to get GHL help, what each typically costs in 2026, and the factors that actually move the number up or down. We will be straight with you: ranges below are typical market figures, not fixed quotes, and your real cost depends entirely on scope.

The Three Ways to Hire GoHighLevel Help

Before talking money, it helps to understand who you are actually comparing. Most buyers choose between a freelancer, an in-house employee, or a specialist agency. Each solves a different problem.

Option 1: The Freelancer (Upwork, Fiverr, Facebook groups)

A GHL freelancer is the cheapest and most flexible entry point. You can find people who will install a snapshot, wire up a basic funnel, or build a single workflow on a per-task basis.

  • Typical 2026 rates: roughly $20–$75 per hour for general help, with experienced specialists charging $75–$150+. Small fixed-price gigs (a snapshot install, one funnel) often land in the $100–$800 range.
  • Pros: low cost, fast to start, easy to scale up or down, and great for one-off tasks where you know exactly what you need.
  • Cons: quality varies wildly, there is little continuity if they disappear, and most freelancers are strong in one area (funnels) but not full-stack across automations, AI agents, and SaaS Mode. You are also the project manager.

Freelancers are a smart pick when the task is small, well-defined, and you can afford to test a few people until you find one who is reliable.

Option 2: The In-House Hire

Bringing a GHL specialist onto your payroll gives you a dedicated person who lives inside your account every day.

  • Typical 2026 cost: a skilled full-time GoHighLevel operator commonly runs $50,000–$90,000+ per year in the US, plus benefits, taxes, software, and management time. Part-time or offshore hires cost less but still carry recruiting and training overhead.
  • Pros: fully dedicated, deep knowledge of your business, and available for daily fires and ongoing optimization.
  • Cons: expensive, and genuinely skilled GHL people are hard to find — the platform changes fast and one person rarely covers automations, custom dev, AI, and SaaS Mode at once. If they leave, your knowledge walks out the door.

An in-house hire makes sense once GHL is core to your operation and you have enough recurring work to keep someone busy full time.

Option 3: The Specialist Agency (like GHL Prime)

A specialist agency gives you a full team — setup, automation, AI, and development — instead of betting on one individual. This is the route most agencies and growing businesses settle on once GHL becomes mission-critical.

  • One-time setup projects: typical 2026 ranges run from around $1,500 for a focused build to $10,000+ for a complex, multi-system setup with snapshots, automations, and integrations.
  • Monthly retainers: ongoing management and optimization commonly sits in the $750–$3,500+ per month range depending on volume and how hands-on the work is.
  • White-label support: if you resell GHL, white-label tech support and build services are usually priced per seat or as a monthly package so you can offer expert help under your own brand.
  • Pros: certified, full-stack, with continuity and a documented process. You are not exposed if one person quits.
  • Cons: higher than a bargain-bin freelancer — you are paying for a team and reliability, not the lowest hourly rate.

What Actually Drives the Price

Whichever route you choose, scope is the real lever. Two projects both called ‘GoHighLevel setup’ can differ by 10x because of what is inside them. Here is what moves the number.

  • Setup depth: a single funnel and pipeline is cheap; a full account build with domains, email/SMS deliverability, calendars, and forms is a real project.
  • Snapshots: installing an existing snapshot is fast and inexpensive. Building a custom, reusable snapshot from scratch costs more because it is engineering, not just configuration.
  • Automations and workflows: the more triggers, conditions, and integrations you need, the more design and testing time it takes — this is where hours add up quietly.
  • SaaS Mode and SaaS CRM: launching SaaS Mode with rebilling, plans, and onboarding is a significantly bigger lift than a single-business setup.
  • AI voice agents: conversational AI and voice agents require scripting, training, and integration, which sit at the higher end.
  • Custom development: custom code, API work, and bespoke features (what we call ‘Vibe Coding’) are the biggest price driver because they are true software builds.

When you ask for a quote, the most useful thing you can do is describe the outcome you want — not just ‘set up GHL.’ The clearer the scope, the tighter and more honest the price.

How to Decide

There is no single right answer, only the right fit for your situation. A quick way to think about it: choose a freelancer for small, one-off tasks; consider an in-house hire when GHL is daily, central work and you can keep someone fully occupied; and pick a specialist agency when you need full-stack expertise, continuity, and someone accountable for the whole system — without building and managing a team yourself.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is a cheap GHL freelancer ever worth it?

Yes, for narrow, well-defined tasks. The risk is rework — a $200 build that breaks can cost more to fix than doing it right once. Vet carefully and start small.

What is a typical GoHighLevel consultant price?

Independent consultants commonly charge $75–$200+ per hour in 2026, while agencies tend to quote per project or per month so your cost is tied to outcomes rather than the clock.

Why does agency pricing beat a $20 freelancer over time?

Because you stop paying twice. A full-stack team builds it correctly, documents it, and supports it — so you avoid the cycle of cheap builds, breakage, and re-hiring.

Can you give me an exact number now?

Not honestly, until we know your scope. A focused setup and a full SaaS Mode launch with custom dev are different worlds. That is exactly what a short consultation sorts out.

Get a Real Quote, Not a Guess

The honest answer to ‘how much does it cost to hire a GoHighLevel expert’ is: it depends on what you are building — and you deserve a number based on your actual goals, not a generic price tag. blogPosts.excerpt: A practical round-up of GoHighLevel niche integrations: connect Houzz, Adobe, ServiceTitan, Jotform, CallRail and more to GHL via Zapier or webhooks.
blogPosts.content:
GoHighLevel is the hub of your marketing and sales, but most agencies run a stack of industry tools that GHL has never heard of. The good news: you almost never need a native connector. With Zapier, webhooks, or a small piece of custom middleware, you can pipe leads, jobs, and signed documents from nearly any platform straight into GHL as contacts, opportunities, or workflow triggers.

This is a round-up of GoHighLevel niche integrations we get asked about most. For each tool we cover the trigger–action pattern, and at the end we explain what to do when a tool isn’t even on Zapier. In Zapier, remember that GoHighLevel appears under its older product name, LeadConnector — that’s the app you search for when adding GHL as an action.

The general pattern for GoHighLevel industry integrations

Almost every integration below follows the same shape. Something happens in the source tool (a new lead, a completed job, a signed agreement) — that’s the trigger. Zapier catches it and runs an action in LeadConnector: create or update a contact, add a tag, or fire an inbound webhook that starts a workflow. Once the contact lands in GHL with the right tags, your automations — nurture sequences, pipeline moves, AI follow-up — take over from there.

Houzz: capture renovation leads as GHL contacts

Houzz Pro is where a lot of home-renovation and design firms field inquiries, but those leads do you no good sitting in a separate inbox. Houzz Pro has a Zapier app, so you can bridge it to GHL without custom code.

  • Trigger: a new lead in Houzz Pro (the ‘Houzz Zapier highlevel’ flow most agencies want).
  • Action: create or update a contact in LeadConnector with the name, email, phone, and project details, then apply a tag like ‘houzz-lead’.
  • Result: the contact drops into a GHL workflow that sends an instant reply and books a consult — so a Houzz inquiry gets a response in minutes, not days.

Adobe Acrobat Sign: turn signed documents into contact updates

If you send proposals or contracts through Adobe Acrobat Sign, the signature event is a high-value moment your CRM should know about. Acrobat Sign exposes Zapier triggers for agreements that are created, sent, and completed.

  • Trigger: the ‘Agreement signed’ (completed) event in Adobe Acrobat Sign. This is the core of the ‘Zapier send forms submitted in Adobe to GHL’ use case.
  • Action: update the matching GHL contact — move them to a ‘Signed’ pipeline stage, add a tag, and trigger onboarding.
  • Bonus: Acrobat Sign lets you pull the signed agreement’s form-field data, so values a signer typed (name, address, plan selected) can map straight onto GHL custom fields.

ServiceTitan: sync field-service jobs for marketing follow-up

ServiceTitan runs the operational side of HVAC, plumbing, and electrical businesses — dispatch, jobs, invoicing. GHL runs the marketing side. Connecting the two means every customer ServiceTitan touches can be nurtured for reviews, maintenance reminders, and repeat work. ServiceTitan now has its own Zapier app with triggers for new customers and new jobs.

  • Trigger: a new customer or new/completed job in ServiceTitan.
  • Action: create or update the contact in GHL and tag by job type or completion status.
  • Result: the ‘ServiceTitan GoHighLevel’ sync feeds a post-service review request and a 6-month maintenance follow-up automatically.

Form tools: Jotform, Typeform, and Google Forms

Form builders are the easiest GoHighLevel niche integrations because every major one is on Zapier, and they all follow an identical pattern.

Jotform

  • Trigger: a new Jotform submission.
  • Action: create a GHL contact, map each form field to a custom field, and tag by form.

Typeform

  • Trigger: a new Typeform entry — great for quizzes and qualification surveys.
  • Action: create the contact and branch your GHL workflow on the answers (for example, route ‘ready to buy’ respondents to a sales pipeline).

Google Forms

  • Trigger: a new Google Forms response.
  • Action: push the contact into GHL so even a free, lightweight form feeds your CRM and nurture.

CallRail: attach call tracking to the right contact

Phone calls are leads too. CallRail tracks the calls your campaigns generate, and its Zapier app lets that data reach GHL so a caller becomes a tracked contact with the source attached.

  • Trigger: a new CallRail call (or a completed call with recording and source data).
  • Action: create or update the GHL contact, store the call source and campaign in custom fields, and tag missed calls for instant text-back.
  • Result: you can see which campaign drove each call and follow up before the lead goes cold.

What if my tool isn’t on Zapier?

Plenty of niche and industry platforms have no Zapier app at all. You still have two reliable paths.

  • Webhooks: if the tool can send an outbound webhook when something happens, point it at a GHL inbound-webhook trigger or at Zapier’s ‘Webhooks by Zapier’ catch hook. From there you map the payload into LeadConnector exactly like any other Zap.
  • Custom middleware: when there’s no Zapier app and no webhook, we build a small connector that talks to the tool’s API on one side and the GHL API on the other — running on a schedule or in real time. This is also the right call when you need two-way sync, heavy field mapping, or logic Zapier can’t express cleanly.

Frequently asked questions

Does GoHighLevel have native integrations for these tools?

Mostly no. GHL has native connectors for a short list of major platforms, but Houzz, Adobe Acrobat Sign, ServiceTitan, and most industry tools connect through Zapier (as LeadConnector), webhooks, or custom code instead.

Is Zapier always the best option?

It’s the fastest for one-directional, low-volume flows. For high volume, two-way sync, or complex mapping, a custom connector is usually cheaper to run and more reliable.

Can these run in real time?

Webhook- and trigger-based Zaps fire within seconds. Tools that only offer polling or scheduled exports will have a short delay, which we account for in the design.

Whatever sits in your stack, we can get it talking to GoHighLevel — native, Zapier, webhook, or a custom-built connector when there’s no other way. blogPosts.title: GoHighLevel Voice AI Voice Cloning: Clone Your Voice (2026)
blogPosts.author: GHL Prime Team
blogPosts.excerpt: A practical 2026 guide to GHL Voice AI clone: how to clone a voice for your AI agent, when to use it, quality tips, and the consent and ethics rules you must follow.
blogPosts.content:
For years, AI phone agents had a tell — the voice. Capable on logic, but generic and obviously synthetic. In 2026 that gap is closing fast, and GoHighLevel now lets you build a Voice AI agent that speaks in a cloned, human-sounding voice you choose. Done right, it’s the difference between “clearly a robot” and “sounds like our team.”

This guide covers what GHL Voice AI voice cloning is, how it works, when to clone versus pick a stock voice, the quality tips that matter, and — most importantly — the consent and ethics rules you cannot skip.

What voice cloning in GHL Voice AI is — and why it matters in 2026

GoHighLevel’s Voice AI is part of the AI Employee toolset that answers and places calls for receptionist and outbound use cases. Historically you assigned one of several stock voices to an agent. Voice cloning changes that: you can create a custom AI voice from a short, clean recording and assign it to an agent — so your after-hours line, your booking bot, or your outbound follow-up agent speaks in a branded, recognizable voice.

Why it matters now: callers are sensitive to the “uncanny robot” feeling, and a familiar, on-brand voice builds trust faster. For agencies running calls across many clients, a consistent voice keeps the brand experience tight from first ring to booked appointment.

One honest note up front: voice cloning in HighLevel is an emerging capability that has been rolling out through Labs. The exact menus and toggles can change, and it may not be generally available in every account yet. Treat the steps below as a sensible map, not a permanent click-path.

How GHL voice cloning generally works

The core idea is simple and consistent across the AI voice space: you provide a clean sample of the target voice, the system processes it into a reusable cloned voice, and you assign that voice to an agent. In HighLevel today the flow generally looks like this:

  • Enable the feature: Because it has shipped via Labs, you (or an agency admin) may need to turn on the relevant Voice AI cloning toggle in your settings before the option appears.
  • Add a custom voice: In the Voice AI voice selection screen, under your “My Voices” area, choose to add a custom voice and select the clone option.
  • Provide the sample: Name the voice, pick a provider, then upload or record an audio sample.
  • Let it process: Submitted clones show a processing state while the voice is generated, then appear in your custom voice library.
  • Assign and test: Attach the cloned voice to a Voice AI agent and run real test calls before going live.

Heads up on limits: imported and cloned voices typically share a combined cap (around ten per company at the time of writing), so curate your library rather than cloning everyone in the office.

Honest setup guidance

You don’t need a studio, but you do need discipline. The single biggest factor in a usable clone is the quality of your source recording.

Record a quality sample

  • Quiet room, no echo: Kill background noise, fans, and hard surfaces that bounce sound. One speaker only — no overlapping voices.
  • Enough length and variety: Aim for a few minutes of natural speech. Include normal sentences, a few questions, and some warmth and energy so the clone learns your real range, not a monotone read.
  • Natural pacing: Speak the way you’d talk to a customer on the phone. Over-enunciating or reading robotically produces a robotic clone.
  • Clean input: A decent USB or phone mic close to your mouth beats a laptop mic across the room.

Assign the voice and test on calls

Once the clone finishes processing, assign it to your agent and place test calls to yourself. Listen for mispronounced names, weird emphasis, and pacing. Tune the agent’s prompt and, if needed, re-record a better sample. Never push a freshly cloned voice straight to live customers without hearing it on an actual phone connection — calls compress audio differently than your browser preview.

Clone your voice or use a high-quality stock voice?

Cloning is powerful, but it’s not always the right call.

  • Clone when the voice is the brand: A solo owner or a recognizable spokesperson whose personal voice builds trust — an after-hours receptionist that sounds like the owner is a strong use case.
  • Clone for consistency at scale: When you want one identical brand voice across inbound and outbound campaigns rather than a patchwork of stock voices.
  • Use a stock voice when speed and neutrality matter: If you just need a professional, friendly agent fast — or you don’t have clear rights to a specific person’s voice — a high-quality stock voice is the safer, simpler choice.
  • Use a stock voice for multi-client agencies without permission: Never clone a client’s voice on a hunch. Stock voices carry none of that legal risk.

Consent and ethics: read this before you clone anyone

This is the part that protects you. Voice cloning sits on top of privacy, biometric, and publicity laws, and 2026 enforcement is real.

  • Only clone a voice you have explicit permission to use. Clear, informed, written consent from the person whose voice it is — including what the voice will be used for. Cloning your own voice? Fine. Cloning a client, employee, or public figure without documented permission? Don’t.
  • Public audio is not consent. A podcast clip or YouTube video being online does not give you the right to clone that voice. Implied or assumed consent creates real legal exposure.
  • Disclose that callers are talking to AI. Regulators increasingly expect clear disclosure when a synthetic voice is used in consumer-facing contexts. Undisclosed AI voices can be treated as deceptive and erode trust fast.
  • Know your jurisdiction. Rules differ by region — the EU, UK, and various US states each have their own consent and disclosure expectations — and call-recording consent laws still apply on top. When in doubt, get qualified legal advice; this article is guidance, not legal counsel.

The ethical bar is simple: clone voices you own or have explicit permission for, tell people they’re speaking with an AI, and never use a cloned voice to impersonate or deceive.

Limitations to expect

  • Beta behavior: As a Labs-stage feature, availability, menus, and provider options can shift without notice.
  • Garbage in, garbage out: A noisy or short sample yields a flat, off clone — the recording is the bottleneck, not the AI.
  • Voice library caps: Shared limits mean you can’t hoard unlimited cloned voices per account.
  • Not a personality: A great voice on a weak prompt still gives a weak experience. The agent’s script and logic matter as much as how it sounds.

Frequently asked questions

Is GHL voice cloning available to everyone?

Not necessarily. It has rolled out through Labs, so it may need enabling by an admin and might not appear in every account yet. Check your Voice AI and Labs settings, or ask us to confirm what’s live.

How long should my voice sample be?

A few minutes of clean, varied speech from a single speaker is a good target. More natural variety generally produces a more realistic, less robotic clone.

Can I clone a client’s or employee’s voice?

Only with their explicit, documented permission for that specific use. Without it, use a high-quality stock voice instead.

Do I have to tell callers it’s an AI?

Best practice — and increasingly the legal expectation — is yes. Clear disclosure builds trust and keeps you on the right side of consumer-protection rules.

Want a branded voice agent done right?

Voice cloning is the easy part; the hard part is a Voice AI agent that books appointments, follows up, and stays compliant. We build and manage exactly that. Explore our AI agent builder service to see how we set up branded voice agents end to end — or contact us and we’ll map the right voice strategy for your business.

blogPosts.title: GoHighLevel + Stripe: Setup, Rebilling & Subscriptions Guide
blogPosts.author: GHL Prime Team
blogPosts.excerpt: A complete guide to GoHighLevel Stripe integration: connect Stripe, sell products and subscriptions, set up SaaS Mode rebilling, and fix the connection problems that break payments.
blogPosts.content:
Stripe is the engine behind almost every dollar that moves through GoHighLevel. Get the GoHighLevel Stripe integration right and you can take card payments, run recurring subscriptions, and bill your own SaaS clients without touching a separate billing tool. Get it wrong — test keys in live, the wrong Stripe account, missing webhook events — and payments silently fail while you wonder where the revenue went.

This guide walks through both jobs Stripe does inside GHL: collecting client-facing payments, and powering SaaS Mode agency billing. We’ll cover setup, subscriptions, where Stripe webhooks fit, the connection problems we see most often, and how to fix them.

The two distinct jobs Stripe does in GoHighLevel

It helps to keep these separate in your head, because they live in different places and have different rules.

  • Client-facing payments: selling your own products and services — one-time charges, invoices, and subscriptions — through order forms, the payments area, and invoicing. This is connected inside a sub-account.
  • SaaS Mode agency billing: charging the agencies and businesses you resell GoHighLevel to. This is connected at the agency level and is what makes rebilling and recurring plan charges work.

Both run on Stripe, but you configure them independently. A common mistake is assuming one connection covers both — it doesn’t.

How to connect Stripe to GoHighLevel

To handle gohighlevel payments in a sub-account, go to Payments > Integrations. Alongside Stripe you’ll see PayPal, Authorize.net, NMI, and Square, but Stripe is the primary processor and the only one that supports SaaS Mode. Click Connect with Stripe, log into (or create) your Stripe account, and authorize the connection so the two systems sync.

Once connected, one detail catches people out: GoHighLevel only tracks transactions created through GoHighLevel after you connect. Payments you took directly in Stripe before the integration will not back-fill into your GHL reporting. Your numbers start from the connection date forward.

Test mode vs live mode

Stripe gives you two sets of API keys: test and live. Test mode lets you run fake card numbers through your funnels to confirm everything works before real money is involved. When you’re ready to sell, you must switch to live keys. Leaving test-mode keys connected in a live environment is the single most common reason “working” checkouts take no money — the page submits, but nothing ever hits a real card.

Selling products, invoices, and subscriptions

With Stripe connected, you can sell in several ways:

  • Order forms: attach a product to a funnel or standalone order form for a one-time or recurring charge at checkout.
  • Invoices: send one-off or recurring invoices from the Payments area — useful for services billed manually or on a schedule.
  • Products & subscriptions: define products with recurring pricing so Stripe charges the customer automatically each cycle.

How GHL Stripe subscriptions actually work

When a customer buys a recurring product, GoHighLevel creates a subscription in Stripe and Stripe handles the recurring charge on each billing cycle. GHL reads the initial subscription state directly from Stripe at signup — that verified response is the source of truth for whether the subscription started cleanly. From there, Stripe keeps GoHighLevel updated about renewals, failed payments, and cancellations as they happen. This is exactly where webhooks come in.

Where Stripe webhooks fit

A webhook is just a message Stripe sends to GoHighLevel when something happens — a payment succeeds, a subscription renews, a card is declined, a customer cancels. For stripe webhooks ghl you generally don’t configure these by hand; the official connection wires them up for you. Their job is to keep GHL in sync after the initial sale and to act as a fallback if the first verification ever fails.

When webhook events go missing, you get ghosts: a subscription that renewed in Stripe but still shows as failed in GHL, or a cancellation that never updated the contact. If your records and Stripe disagree, missing or misrouted webhook events are usually the cause — and reconnecting the integration through the proper flow re-establishes them.

SaaS Mode billing and rebilling

SaaS Mode is how you resell GoHighLevel as your own branded platform and bill clients on a recurring plan. To connect Stripe to GoHighLevel for this, you link Stripe at the agency level — Stripe is currently the only supported provider for SaaS billing. SaaS Mode and rebilling require the $497 Agency Pro plan; they are not available on the $97 or $297 tiers.

Rebilling lets you charge clients for usage — email, phone, SMS, AI, premium workflow actions — with your own markup on top of the wholesale cost. You enable it in agency settings, toggle on rebilling, and set a markup. Recurring plan charges and usage billing both flow through that agency Stripe connection.

One hard rule trips up almost everyone the first time: both the agency account and each client sub-account must use live Stripe keys. If a sub-account is connected with test-mode keys, new sub-accounts won’t generate from your SaaS order form and billing won’t trigger. Rebilling is deep enough to deserve its own treatment, but the foundation is always a clean, live Stripe connection on both sides.

Common connection problems and how to fix them

  • Test-mode keys in a live environment: checkouts succeed visually but take no money, or SaaS sub-accounts never generate. Switch to live keys on every account involved.
  • Wrong Stripe account connected: payments land in the wrong place, or agency and sub-account use mismatched accounts. Disconnect and reconnect the intended account.
  • Failed or declined payments: often expired cards, insufficient funds, or Stripe’s fraud rules. Check the failure reason in the Stripe dashboard before assuming GHL is broken.
  • Missing webhook events: GHL and Stripe records drift out of sync. Reconnect through Payments > Integrations to restore the event flow.
  • Currency mismatch: your Stripe account currency must match what your products and plans charge in, or transactions get rejected.

When in doubt, treat the Stripe dashboard as the source of truth for what actually happened, and GoHighLevel as the system that should reflect it. Most “GHL bug” reports turn out to be a key, an account, or a webhook issue.

Frequently asked questions

Can I use one Stripe account for both client payments and SaaS billing?

You can use the same Stripe business, but the connections are configured separately — one in the sub-account for client payments, one at the agency level for SaaS Mode. Connecting one does not automatically cover the other.

Do I need Agency Pro just to take client payments?

No. Connecting Stripe in a sub-account to sell products, invoices, and subscriptions works on standard plans. The $497 Agency Pro plan is required specifically for SaaS Mode and rebilling.

Why do my GHL reports not match my Stripe totals?

Usually because GoHighLevel only tracks transactions created through GHL after you connected, or because some webhook events didn’t arrive. Pre-connection Stripe payments never sync in.

Is Stripe the only payment option?

For SaaS Mode, yes. For client-facing payments you can also use PayPal, Authorize.net, NMI, or Square, but Stripe is the most capable and the default choice for subscriptions.

Get your payments built right the first time

A clean Stripe setup is the difference between a SaaS that bills clients automatically and one that quietly loses revenue. We connect Stripe, configure subscriptions and rebilling, and test every flow in both modes before you go live. If you want this done correctly from day one, explore our SaaS CRM launch service or get in touch and we’ll map out your payments and billing setup.

blogPosts.title: GoHighLevel AI Studio: Custom Code, JavaScript & API
blogPosts.author: GHL Prime Team
blogPosts.excerpt: A practical guide to extending GoHighLevel AI Studio with custom code, JavaScript and the GHL API v2 – where code lives, how to use contact_id and location_id, and real examples.
blogPosts.content:
GoHighLevel’s AI Studio lets you describe a website or funnel in plain language and watch it build itself. That speed is genuinely useful, but at some point you hit the edge of what point-and-click can do — a real-time quote calculator, a form that pre-fills from the logged contact, or a submission that posts to your own API. That’s where custom code, JavaScript and the GHL API v2 come in.

This guide is for builders who want to extend the gohighlevel ai studio website builder with custom code, javascript and the api — cleanly, securely and in the right place. We’ll show you exactly where code lives, how to grab the identifiers you need, and three real things you can ship this week.

Where custom code lives in GoHighLevel

There isn’t one magic box. GHL gives you several injection points, and choosing the right one matters for both behavior and security.

  • The Custom Code / Custom JS-HTML element: Drop this element onto any page or funnel step in the builder and paste raw HTML, CSS and JavaScript. This is the home for widgets — calculators, embedded apps, interactive UI. AI Studio even ships a built-in Code Editor so you can edit the code behind an AI-generated project directly.
  • Page / funnel Header & Footer tracking code: Found in the page or funnel settings, these fields inject scripts site-wide or step-wide. Use the header for things that must load early (a font, a config object) and the footer for scripts that should run after the page renders.
  • The workflow Custom Code action: This runs server-side JavaScript inside a workflow, not in the browser. You pass values in through an InputData object — mapped from merge fields and previous steps — and run logic safely away from the visitor’s eyes. This is where secret API calls belong.

The AI website builder and its code injection points

The AI website builder (part of AI Studio) generates a working project from a prompt, a URL or a reference design. You don’t lose control once it’s built: the Code Editor exposes the underlying files so you can adjust markup, styles and behavior, and on a standard funnel or website you still have the Custom Code element plus the Header/Footer fields.

A simple mental model: use AI Studio to generate the structure fast, then layer javascript in gohighlevel on top through the element or footer for the interactive parts the AI can’t infer. The ai website builder ghl gives you the skeleton; your code gives it behavior.

Getting identifiers: contact_id and location_id

The moment you want code to talk to GHL data, you need two identifiers, and confusing them is the most common mistake we see.

  • contact_id identifies a single contact (a person) inside a sub-account. You use it when reading or updating one record — fetching a contact’s details, adding a tag, updating a custom field.
  • location_id identifies the sub-account (the “location”) itself. The API uses it to scope your request to the right account, and almost every v2 endpoint expects it in the path or body.

You expose these to your code through merge fields / custom values. On a page, GHL can render the current contact and location identifiers into the markup; in a workflow Custom Code action, you map them into InputData using the custom value picker. The pair — contact_id location_id — is what lets your script know who it’s acting on and where.

How to read them in front-end code

In a Custom Code element, you typically read a merge field that GHL has rendered into the page (for example, writing the contact id into a hidden input or a small JavaScript config object in the footer), then reference it from your script. Treat anything the browser can see as public — never put a private key next to it.

Calling the GHL API v2 from custom code

GHL’s API v2 is the current standard (v1 reached end-of-support at the end of 2025). It’s a REST API: you make authenticated requests to endpoints for contacts, conversations, calendars, payments and more, and you scope them with the identifiers above.

The critical rule: where you call it from decides everything.

  • Server-side (the workflow Custom Code action): Safe to authenticate and call the API here. Your token never reaches the browser. This is the right place to enrich a contact, sync data or trigger an external system.
  • Browser-side (the Custom Code element): Anything here is visible to the visitor. Never embed a secret API key, private token or anything that grants account access in front-end code. If a widget needs server data, have it call a small endpoint you control (or a webhook) that holds the secret instead.

The pattern we use repeatedly: the front-end widget collects input and the contact_id, then posts to a Webhook or your own serverless function; that function (with the secret safely stored) calls the GHL API v2 using the location_id to scope the request. Front-end stays dumb and public; secrets stay server-side.

Three real things you can build

1. A custom calculator / quote widget

Drop a Custom Code element onto a funnel step with a few inputs — square footage, headcount, plan tier — and write JavaScript that computes a live price as the user types. It’s pure front-end math, no secrets needed, and it dramatically lifts conversion versus a static price table. Write the final number into a hidden form field so it’s captured on submit.

2. Pre-filling a form from a contact

When a known contact lands on a page (say, from an email link), render their details via merge fields and use a short footer script to populate the form — name, email, current plan. Read the rendered contact_id so the submission updates the right record. Less typing means more completed forms.

3. Posting data to an external API on submit

Attach a submit handler in a Custom Code element that, on form submission, posts the captured data to an external system — your CRM, an inventory tool, a Slack alert. For anything requiring a secret, route it through a workflow Webhook or Custom Code action so the credential lives server-side, not in the visitor’s browser.

FAQ

Can I run server-side code without an external server?

Yes — the workflow Custom Code action runs JavaScript server-side inside GHL, with values passed in through InputData. For heavier or external logic, a webhook to a serverless function gives you more room.

Is it safe to call the GHL API from a Custom Code element on a page?

Only for requests that don’t require a secret. Anything in a page element is public. Keep tokens and private keys in the workflow Custom Code action or a server you control.

Do I always need both contact_id and location_id?

You almost always need location_id to scope a v2 request to the right sub-account. You add contact_id whenever the action targets a specific person.

Will my custom code survive an AI Studio regeneration?

Edits made in the Code Editor persist, but re-prompting the AI to rebuild a section can overwrite it. Keep critical custom logic in clearly separated elements or footer scripts so it’s easy to re-apply.

Ship it without the guesswork

Extending AI Studio is where GHL goes from a fast site builder to a genuine application platform — but the line between front-end and server-side, and the handling of identifiers and secrets, is exactly where most builds break or leak. blogPosts.title: Zapier & GHL Automation: What It Is + 10 Workflows to Build
blogPosts.author: GHL Prime Team
blogPosts.excerpt: A plain-English guide to what Zapier & GHL automation is, when to use it versus native GHL workflows, and 10 specific no-code workflows you can build today.
blogPosts.content:
If you run an agency or a growing business on GoHighLevel, you have probably hit a wall: GHL handles everything inside your CRM beautifully, but at some point you need it to talk to an app that lives outside of it. That is where Zapier comes in. In this guide we explain plainly what Zapier & GHL automation is, when to reach for it instead of a native GHL workflow, and 10 specific workflows you can build with no code.

Let’s define the pieces first, because the term ‘automation’ gets thrown around loosely.

What is Zapier & GHL automation?

Zapier is a no-code integration platform that connects thousands of apps together. It works on a simple model: a trigger (something happens in one app) kicks off one or more actions (something happens in another app). A single automation is called a ‘Zap’. You build it by pointing and clicking — no developers required.

GoHighLevel (GHL) is an all-in-one CRM and marketing platform built for agencies and service businesses. It handles contacts, pipelines, calendars, email, SMS, funnels, and its own native automation engine called Workflows.

So what is Zapier & GHL automation? It is the practice of using Zapier to connect GoHighLevel to other apps using triggers and actions, with no code. In Zapier, GHL appears as LeadConnector — the official, white-labeled HighLevel app. You authenticate with your HighLevel login, choose a sub-account, and you can then use triggers like New Contact, New Opportunity, or Pipeline Stage Changed, and actions like Add or Update Contact, Add to Workflow, and Add Task. When the native LeadConnector trigger or action you need does not exist, Zapier’s Webhooks tool fills the gap.

When to use Zapier vs native GHL workflows

This is the question that saves you money and headaches, so here is the rule of thumb: use native GHL workflows for automation that stays inside the platform, and use Zapier when you need to connect to an outside app that GHL does not natively support.

Reach for native GHL workflows when…

The whole automation lives inside GoHighLevel — a new lead triggering an email and SMS sequence, moving an opportunity through a pipeline, booking a calendar slot, assigning a task, or sending an internal notification. GHL workflows are included at no extra cost, your reporting stays unified, and you avoid stitching data across dashboards. As a habit, always check whether GHL can do it natively first.

Reach for Zapier when…

The trigger or the destination lives outside GHL. GHL workflows cannot natively listen to or push data into apps Zapier covers, such as Stripe, Google Sheets, Slack, Calendly, QuickBooks, Airtable, or your own internal tools. When the event happens in one of those apps, or you need to send GHL data into one of them, Zapier catches it and relays it. Used this way, Zapier complements GHL rather than replacing it — GHL stays your core system, and Zapier is the bridge to everything else.

10 Zapier + GHL workflows worth building

Each of these is a single Zap. They are practical, commonly requested, and easy to extend once you understand the trigger-and-action pattern.

1. New GHL lead to a Google Sheets row

Trigger on a new LeadConnector contact, then add a row to a Google Sheet. This GHL Zapier workflow gives sales teams, bookkeepers, or clients a live spreadsheet view without handing out CRM access — perfect for reporting and quick exports.

2. New lead to a Slack channel alert

When a new contact enters GHL, post a message to a Slack channel so your team gets an instant heads-up. Great for high-value inquiries where speed-to-lead matters and nobody should be refreshing the CRM all day.

3. Stripe payment to a GHL contact and tag

When a Stripe payment succeeds, create or update the contact in GHL and apply a tag like paid-customer. Because the payment event happens outside GHL, this is a textbook case for Zapier. The tag can then start a native GHL workflow for onboarding.

4. Calendly or Acuity booking to a GHL appointment and contact

When someone books in Calendly or Acuity, push the contact and booking details into GHL. If your audience prefers an external scheduler, this keeps your CRM as the single source of truth without forcing a tool switch.

5. Typeform or Jotform submission to GHL

Capture a Typeform or Jotform submission and create or update the matching GHL contact, mapping each form field cleanly. Ideal for quizzes, applications, and intake forms hosted outside GHL that still need to feed your pipeline.

6. QuickBooks or Xero invoice to GHL

When a new invoice is created or paid in QuickBooks or Xero, update the contact in GHL — tag them, add a note, or trigger a follow-up. This keeps your finance system and your CRM in sync without manual data entry.

7. Mailchimp subscriber sync

When someone subscribes in Mailchimp, add or update them as a GHL contact (and vice versa). Useful during a migration to GHL, or when a client insists on keeping a legacy Mailchimp list alive while you consolidate.

8. Airtable record sync

When a record is created or updated in Airtable, mirror it into GHL as a contact or opportunity. Plenty of teams run operations in Airtable; this GHL integration via Zapier connects that workspace to your sales and marketing engine.

9. New GHL opportunity to a project tool

When an opportunity is created or its pipeline stage changes in GHL, create a card or task in Asana, Trello, or ClickUp. The moment a deal becomes work, your delivery team sees it — no copy-paste handoff between sales and fulfillment.

10. Inbound webhook to an internal or custom app

Use Zapier’s Webhooks tool to catch an inbound webhook from an internal system or a custom-built app, then create or update records in GHL. This is the catch-all for anything bespoke and the doorway to genuinely custom GoHighLevel Zapier automation.

A few things to keep in mind

GHL’s API has rate limits, so very high-volume syncs need thoughtful design to avoid throttling. Field mapping matters — mismatched fields are the most common reason a Zap silently does the wrong thing. And before you build any of these, ask the native question first: if GHL can do it inside the platform, do it there and save the Zapier seat for the jobs only it can handle.

Build it once, build it right

Done well, Zapier becomes the quiet connective tissue between GoHighLevel and the rest of your stack. Done poorly, it becomes a tangle of half-working Zaps nobody understands. If you would rather have it mapped, built, and documented properly the first time, that is exactly the kind of work we do.

blogPosts.title: Can You Connect GoHighLevel to Claude AI? (3 Methods)
blogPosts.author: GHL Prime Team
blogPosts.excerpt: Yes – you can use Zapier to connect GoHighLevel to Claude, or call the Anthropic API directly from a workflow. Here are three methods, with setup, pros, and cons.
blogPosts.content:
Short answer: yes. You can connect GoHighLevel to Claude, Anthropic’s AI model family, and put it to work scoring leads, drafting replies, and summarising calls inside your existing workflows. The question most people really have is how – and which method fits their tolerance for code, cost, and volume.

Below we walk through three ways to connect the two platforms, from a no-code Zapier setup to a fully custom middleware app. For each, we cover the rough setup, the trade-offs, and where your Anthropic API key lives (and why it must stay secret).

The three ways to connect GoHighLevel to Claude

Every method does the same fundamental thing: it takes data out of GHL (a new lead, an inbound message, a call transcript), sends it to Claude with a prompt, and brings the response back into GHL. They differ only in who does the plumbing and how much control you get.

Method 1: Zapier with LeadConnector + the Anthropic/Claude action (easiest, no code)

This is the answer to the most common question we hear: can I use Zapier to connect GoHighLevel to Claude? Yes – and it’s the fastest route. Zapier has both a GoHighLevel integration (via the LeadConnector app) and an Anthropic/Claude integration, so you can wire them together without writing a line of code.

  • The trigger: Use a LeadConnector trigger such as “New Contact,” “New Inbound Message,” or “Contact Tag Added” to start the Zap.
  • The action: Add an Anthropic (Claude) action, write your prompt, and map GHL fields (name, message body, notes) into it.
  • The return trip: Add a second LeadConnector action to write Claude’s output back – update a custom field, add a note, send an SMS, or apply a tag.

Where the key lives: You connect your Anthropic account to Zapier once, and Zapier stores the API key. You never paste it into GHL. Pros: no code, fast to launch, easy to maintain. Cons: a Zapier task is consumed on every run (cost adds up at volume), and you’re limited to what the pre-built action exposes.

Method 2: A direct webhook or Custom Code call from a GHL workflow (more control)

If you want to skip the middleman and reduce per-task cost, call the Anthropic API directly from a GoHighLevel workflow. GHL workflows include a Custom Code action and inbound/outbound Webhook steps that can reach external APIs – including Anthropic’s messages endpoint at api.anthropic.com.

  • Set up the call: In your workflow, add a webhook or Custom Code action that sends a POST request to the Anthropic messages endpoint. The request carries your API key in a header, a model name, a max-tokens value, and your prompt built from workflow data.
  • Handle the response: Parse Claude’s reply and map it back into a GHL custom field or follow-up step.
  • This is the core GHL AI webhook pattern: one workflow step out to Claude, one step back into your contact record – no third-party automation tool in between.

Where the key lives: Your Anthropic API key is sent in the request header. Treat it like a password – never expose it in a public-facing form, a client-side script, or anywhere a contact could see it. Store it in a workflow setting or a dedicated config field, not in plain view. Pros: more control over the prompt, model, and parsing; no per-task Zapier fee. Cons: you need to be comfortable with API requests, headers, and JSON, and error handling is on you.

Method 3: Custom middleware or an app (advanced, high-volume, multi-account)

When you’re running this across many sub-accounts, handling high request volumes, or need logic that’s too complex for a single workflow step, the right move is a small middleware service sitting between GHL and Anthropic.

  • What it does: GHL sends events to your service; your service calls the Anthropic API with full control over retries, rate limits, caching, logging, and routing; then it writes results back to the right GHL account.
  • Why it scales: You centralise the API key, enforce guardrails, batch requests, and reuse one integration across every client account – ideal for agencies in SaaS Mode.

Where the key lives: Server-side, in a secrets manager or environment variable – never in GHL and never in client code. This is the most secure of the three. Pros: maximum flexibility and reliability at scale. Cons: it’s real software that needs building and maintaining – which is exactly the kind of Vibe Coding custom development we handle for clients.

What to actually use a GoHighLevel + Claude integration for

Connecting the two is only worth it if it does real work. Here are the use cases we deploy most:

  • Lead scoring and qualification: Send a new lead’s details to Claude and have it return a score or a qualified/unqualified flag, then route hot leads to a human instantly.
  • Reply suggestions for staff: Draft a suggested response to an inbound message and drop it into a note so your team can review and send – faster replies without losing the human touch.
  • First-draft content generation: Generate follow-up email drafts, SMS copy, or appointment-reminder variations on demand.
  • Call transcript summaries: Feed a call transcript to Claude and write a tidy summary plus next-step recommendation back to the contact record.
  • Smart routing: Have Claude classify an inbound message by intent (booking, support, billing) and tag the contact so your workflow sends it to the right pipeline.

Example prompt patterns

You don’t need anything elaborate to start. Two patterns that work well:

  • Lead scoring: You are a lead qualification assistant. Given this lead’s name, source, and message, return a score from 1 to 10 and one short sentence explaining why. Lead details: [mapped GHL fields].
  • Reply drafting: Draft a friendly, concise reply to this customer message in our brand voice. Keep it under 60 words and do not invent details we have not provided. Message: [inbound message body].

FAQ

How much does it cost?

You pay Anthropic for API usage based on the tokens (input and output) each request uses, billed through your Anthropic account. With Zapier you also pay per task. A direct webhook avoids the Zapier task fee but still incurs Anthropic usage. Costs scale with volume and prompt size, so keep prompts tight.

Is my data private?

Your data travels to Anthropic’s API over the request. Review Anthropic’s current data-handling and retention policies for your account tier, and avoid sending more personal data than a task genuinely needs. Keep your API key secret at all times – anyone with it can run charges on your account.

Which Claude model should I use?

Anthropic offers several models across the Claude family at different speed, capability, and price points. A faster, lower-cost model is fine for short classification and scoring tasks; a more capable model suits nuanced drafting and summarisation. Start with a cheaper model and step up only if quality demands it.

blogPosts.title: GoHighLevel API & Webhooks: Custom Objects & Approval Flows
blogPosts.author: GHL Prime Team
blogPosts.excerpt: A practical guide to the GoHighLevel API, webhooks, Custom Objects and approval workflows—so your automations push data safely without firing risky messages unreviewed.
blogPosts.content:
The GoHighLevel API is where the platform stops being a CRM and starts being a system you can shape. Connect it well and you can sync records to your own database, push data into billing tools, model business objects that don’t fit a contact, and route risky actions through a human before anything sends. Connect it badly and you get duplicate contacts, leaked tokens, and automations firing messages nobody approved.

This is a developer-leaning guide, but you don’t need to be a backend engineer to follow it. We’ll cover the API v1 sunset and the move to v2, when to use OAuth 2.0 versus Private Integration Tokens, how inbound and outbound webhooks actually work, what Custom Objects unlock, and—most importantly—how to build an approval gate so your automations never auto-send something they shouldn’t.

The API v1 sunset and the move to v2

If you built anything against the GoHighLevel API before 2025, this matters to you. API v1 reached end-of-support on 31 December 2025. Existing v1 connections may still respond, but there are no fixes, no new endpoints, and no support behind them. Anything you build today should target API v2.

API v2 isn’t just a version bump. It uses a modern authorization model, exposes far more of the platform (Custom Objects, conversations, payments, and more), and is the only surface that will keep getting attention. If you’re still running v1 integrations, treat migration as overdue maintenance rather than a someday project—each one is a silent single point of failure.

OAuth 2.0 vs Private Integration Tokens

API v2 gives you two ways to authenticate, and choosing the right one saves a lot of pain later.

  • OAuth 2.0 is for marketplace apps and anything that needs to act across many sub-accounts. The app owner installs it, you receive access and refresh tokens, and your code refreshes them on a schedule. This is the path when you’re building a product other agencies will install, or any integration that spans multiple locations.
  • Private Integration Tokens (PIT) are static tokens scoped to a single sub-account (or the agency level). They behave like a fixed OAuth 2.0 access token, but they do not auto-refresh—you rotate them manually. They’re ideal for internal tools, a single client’s automations, or a server script that only ever touches one location.

The rule of thumb: if it’s your own internal build for one account, reach for a PIT. If it’s a distributable app or it spans accounts, use OAuth 2.0. A few practical notes on PITs—you can create up to five per level, you put the token in the Authorization header like any access token, and you should rotate them on a schedule (every 90 days is a sensible default). Because they don’t expire on their own, a leaked PIT stays valid until you revoke it, so store them as secrets, never in client-side code or a public repo.

Webhooks: inbound triggers and outbound actions

Webhooks are how GoHighLevel talks to the rest of your stack in real time, and there are two directions to keep straight.

  • Inbound webhooks (to start a workflow): an external system POSTs to a GoHighLevel webhook URL, which fires a workflow trigger. This is how you let a form on your own site, a payment processor, or a third-party app kick off automation inside GHL without a single manual step.
  • Outbound webhooks (to push data out): a workflow runs a webhook action that POSTs contact and event data to an endpoint you control. Use this to sync a new lead into your warehouse, notify a Slack channel, trigger a billing event, or hand off to a custom service that does work GHL can’t do natively.

For heavier logic, GoHighLevel’s custom code action lets you run JavaScript inside a workflow—reshaping a payload, calling an external API, or computing a value before the next step. Treat it like any other code: validate inputs, handle the case where a field is missing, and don’t assume the upstream system always sends clean data. Whenever you accept an inbound webhook, verify it’s genuinely from the source you expect rather than acting on any POST that arrives.

Custom Objects: modeling what contacts can’t

Out of the box, GoHighLevel thinks in contacts and opportunities. That’s fine until your business revolves around something else entirely. Custom Objects let you model records that aren’t people—each with their own fields, and linked back to the contacts they relate to.

  • Properties: a real-estate operation can track listings as records—address, price, status, beds, square footage—and associate each with buyers and sellers.
  • Vehicles: a dealership or service shop can store VIN, make, model, mileage and service history against the owner contact.
  • Policies: an insurance agency can model policies with carrier, premium, renewal date and coverage type, then automate renewal reminders off those fields.
  • Projects: an agency or contractor can track projects with scope, stage, budget and deadline, linked to the client and the team.

The payoff is that automations and reporting can run on the real object instead of being crammed into contact custom fields. A renewal workflow that reads a policy’s renewal date is far cleaner—and far harder to break—than one juggling a dozen text fields on a contact.

Build an approval workflow so automations never auto-send

Here’s the failure mode that costs agencies real trust: an automation fires a text or email to a client, a contract, or a high-value lead—without anyone reviewing it. Once it sends, it’s sent. The fix is a human-in-the-loop gate, and GoHighLevel gives you everything you need to build one inside a workflow.

The pattern looks like this:

  • Stop before the risky step: instead of sending the message immediately, the workflow first sends an internal notification to the team—an email, an internal SMS, or a Slack ping via outbound webhook—with the record details and what’s about to go out.
  • Wait for a decision: add a wait step and a condition that checks a status field, for example an Approval Status custom field set to ‘Approved’. The workflow holds until that flag flips.
  • Flip the flag manually: a team member reviews the record and changes the status field (or clicks an approval link that updates it). Only then does the condition pass and the send proceed. If it’s set to ‘Rejected’ or the wait times out, the workflow branches away from sending entirely.

This is the single most valuable safeguard we add to client systems. It turns ‘the automation sent something wrong’ into ‘the automation paused and asked.’ For anything irreversible—outbound client messages, payment actions, contract delivery—the approval gate should be the default, not an afterthought.

Best practices

  • Migrate off v1: build new work on API v2 and retire any lingering v1 calls before they fail quietly.
  • Match auth to scope: PIT for single-account internal tools, OAuth 2.0 for multi-account or marketplace apps.
  • Treat tokens as secrets: never expose a PIT client-side, rotate on a schedule, and revoke immediately if one leaks.
  • Make webhooks idempotent: the same event can arrive twice, so design endpoints that won’t double-create records.
  • Gate risky sends: put an approval condition in front of any outbound message or irreversible action.
  • Validate everything: in custom code, handle missing fields and verify inbound payloads before you act on them.

FAQ

Is GoHighLevel API v1 completely shut off?

It reached end-of-support at the end of 2025. Some calls may still respond, but there are no fixes or support behind them, so you should migrate to v2 and not rely on v1 for anything new.

Do I need OAuth if I’m only working with one account?

No. For a single sub-account, a Private Integration Token is simpler and avoids the refresh-token cycle. Save OAuth 2.0 for multi-account and marketplace builds.

Can I really stop an automation from sending without review?

Yes. A wait step plus a condition on a status field creates a reliable approval gate, so nothing sends until a human flips the flag.

If you want the GoHighLevel API, webhooks, Custom Objects and approval workflows built properly—secure, v2-native, and safe from runaway sends—that’s exactly what our Vibe Coding custom development service is for. blogPosts.title: GoHighLevel and Zapier Integration: How to Connect GHL to 6000+ Apps Without Code
blogPosts.author: GHL Prime Team
blogPosts.excerpt: Connect GoHighLevel to 6000+ apps with Zapier — no code required. Step-by-step setup plus the 5 most valuable GHL Zapier workflows agencies deploy.
blogPosts.content:
GoHighLevel is a powerhouse on its own, but the real magic happens when you connect it to the rest of your stack. With Zapier, you can link GHL to over 6,000 apps — Typeform, Google Sheets, Slack, DocuSign, Stripe and more — without writing a single line of code. In this guide we cover exactly how to set up the GoHighLevel Zapier integration, both the native connection and webhooks, plus the five most valuable GHL Zapier workflows GHL Prime deploys for agency clients every week.

How GoHighLevel Connects to Zapier

There are two ways to connect GHL to Zapier, and knowing when to use each saves you hours of frustration.

  • Native GHL Zapier app — Inside Zapier, search for "HighLevel" or "LeadConnector" (LeadConnector is GoHighLevel's white-label engine). This official app exposes the most common triggers and actions and connects via secure OAuth. It covers roughly 90% of everyday agency use cases.
  • GHL Webhooks — More flexible and built for anything the native app cannot do. Webhooks let you send any data from a GHL workflow to Zapier (and vice versa), so you are never blocked by a missing native trigger.

Rule of thumb: start with the native app, and reach for webhooks the moment you need a trigger or field the native integration does not expose.

Setting Up the Native GHL Zapier Connection

Here is the step-by-step process to wire up the native integration:

  1. Log in to zapier.com and click Create Zap.
  2. In the trigger search box, type HighLevel (or LeadConnector) and select it.
  3. Connect your account via OAuth — Zapier will redirect you to GoHighLevel to authorise access to the correct sub-account.
  4. Choose your trigger event (see the list below).
  5. Click Test trigger so Zapier pulls a real sample record — this is critical for accurate field mapping later.
  6. Add an action step (the app you want to send data to) and map the fields from GHL into that app.
  7. Click Publish to turn the Zap on.

The native GHL trigger events available in Zapier include:

  • New Contact
  • Contact Tag Added
  • Appointment Created
  • Pipeline Stage Changed
  • Form Submitted
  • Invoice Paid

Setting Up GHL Webhooks for Advanced Zaps

Use webhooks when the native triggers do not give you the exact event or data you need — for example, firing only when a contact hits a specific custom condition inside a GHL workflow. Here is how:

  1. In Zapier, create a new Zap and choose Webhooks by Zapier as the trigger, then select Catch Hook.
  2. Copy the webhook URL Zapier generates.
  3. In GoHighLevel, go to Automation > Workflow, add or open a workflow, and click Add Action > Webhook.
  4. Paste the URL into the webhook action and choose the data payload to send.
  5. Trigger the workflow once to send test data so Zapier catches a sample.
  6. Back in Zapier, map the fields from the caught payload into your downstream action.

Webhooks give you total control over the payload, which is why GHL Prime relies on them for complex, multi-condition automations.

Workflow 1 — New Lead from Typeform to GHL Contact

Trigger: Typeform — New Entry. Action: HighLevel — Create Contact. Map the name, email and phone from the Typeform response into the matching GHL contact fields, and add the tag typeform-lead so you can segment these leads instantly.

Bonus: add a second HighLevel action — Add Tag — applying intake-form-submitted. This lets you trigger a GHL nurture workflow the moment the intake form lands, no manual data entry required.

Workflow 2 — GHL Won Deal to Slack Notification

Trigger: HighLevel — Pipeline Stage Changed, with a Zapier Filter step so it only continues when the stage equals Won. Action: Slack — Send Channel Message. Use a message template like:

"New client won: [Contact Name] — [Deal Value]. Assigned to: [Owner]."

Your sales channel celebrates wins in real time and the whole team sees who closed what without anyone opening the CRM.

Workflow 3 — GHL Form Submission to Google Sheets Row

Trigger: HighLevel — Form Submitted. Action: Google Sheets — Create Spreadsheet Row. Map name, email, phone, form name and submission date into columns.

This is excellent as a lightweight CRM backup and reporting layer — every lead lands in a sheet you can filter, pivot or share with stakeholders who do not have GHL access.

Workflow 4 — Stripe Payment to GHL Tag + Pipeline Move

Trigger: Stripe — Payment Succeeded (Charge). Then chain three HighLevel actions:

  1. Add Tag — apply payment-received.
  2. Update Pipeline Stage — move the opportunity to Onboarding.
  3. Send SMS — fire a welcome text to the new paying client.

The result is a fully automated handoff: the second a payment clears, the customer is tagged, advanced in your pipeline and greeted — with zero human involvement.

Workflow 5 — Calendly Booking to GHL Contact + Appointment

Trigger: Calendly — Invitee Created. Actions: first HighLevel — Create or Update Contact (mapping name, email and phone so you never create duplicates), then HighLevel — Create Appointment, mapping the booking date, time and event type.

This keeps your GHL calendar and CRM perfectly in sync with Calendly, so reminders, follow-ups and reporting all run off a single source of truth.

Zapier vs GHL Native Webhooks — Which Should You Use?

FactorZapierGHL Native Webhook
Setup difficultyEasyMedium
CostPaid Zapier plan required for multi-stepFree (built into GHL)
App connections6,000+ apps out of the boxAny app that accepts a webhook
SpeedSeconds (polling/processing)Instant
Best forNon-technical teamsDevelopers and complex flows

For most agencies, Zapier is the fastest route to value. When you need raw speed, zero per-task cost or bespoke logic, native webhooks win.

Common Zapier + GHL Mistakes

  • Hitting free plan limits — Zapier's free tier caps you at 2-step Zaps and around 100 tasks per month; multi-action workflows above need a paid plan.
  • Not testing with real data — skipping the test step leads to broken field mapping that only surfaces once live leads are lost.
  • Forgetting to turn the Zap on — a built-but-unpublished Zap does nothing.
  • Mapping fields wrong — sending an email into a phone field (or worse) corrupts your CRM data.
  • Not monitoring failed Zaps — check Zapier's Zap History regularly so silent failures do not pile up unnoticed.
